doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

title: Hank Jones failing to show up: Goodman's fight and the Barbados recording
summary: Hank Jones's no-shows with Goodman and later for Appleyard's Barbados and Swiss dates, and how they managed without him.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: Well why would he — conversely why would he fire somebody at a moment’s notice? Do you know?

Well sometimes people were taken to task. I never really saw him lose his temper, but Hank Jones, who is my favorite pianist, I mean he was so beautiful, incredible player, and Dick feels the same way, on that record, you know, he’s on that record that I sent you. He was booked to be with us at some special function for the government and didn’t show up. He told Benny that he’d been held up at the George Washington Bridge and couldn’t make it. Benny called the New York Port Authority and found out there was no hold up on the bridge that day. So the next time he came to the states Benny took him to task and they started a fight on the stage. Not physically, but Hank, Hank was very genteel and very proper, and he was cursing at Benny. So he walked off the stage. Benny never used him again. Then on three occasions I booked Hank Jones and he didn’t show up. The record I made over in Barbados was done with Bucky, Major Holly, Butch Miles, Rick Wilkins on tenor, and myself, without the piano. He was booked to play in Barbados. They even rented a German Steinway for him. And I called him two nights before we were to go on, because he was at Carnegie Hall with Ella. I said, “Hank, we’ve got a room at the airport on the night before the flight. We’d like you to be there with us so we can all leave early in the morning.” “Oh, I’ll be there,” he said, “what kind of shoes do you want me to wear?” I said, “I don’t care if you come in your bare feet but be there.” “Oh, I’ll be there.” He didn’t show up. So when we got to Barbados I had to make excuses for him. So I called him back again and I said, “What happened?” He said, “I forgot my passport.” So then he said, “Well I’ll be on the plane tomorrow.” So we drove all the way across the island to pick him up, he didn’t show up. So I called him again, I said, “Hank, what are you doing?” “Oh,” he said, “I didn’t like the attitude of the clerk.”
He said, what? I didn’t follow you.
He didn’t like the airlines clerk, so he said.

So then my friend said he would send a private plane to pick him up in Albany and fly him down to Kennedy, and he didn’t show up. I get to Switzerland, I booked him in Switzerland to play with us. No Hank Jones. “Hank, what happened?” “Oh my car broke down on the way to the airport.” “Oh, Hank,” you know. Anyway, he finally showed up and strangely enough I’d booked him before in Toronto and he didn’t show up again. He claimed he couldn’t get out of here, out of New York, for the weather. And I got this guy Ian Barge to sub. So with the thing in Switzerland it so happened that Ian was working there and he said, “what happened? Didn’t Hank Jones show up?” So now in Barbados I’m stuck. We had four days grace to get a pianist. I called John Bunch. And John said, “What happened, didn’t Hank Jones show up?” “Yeah.” I said, “How did you know.” He said, “I knew about the gig.” He said, “I can’t come, I’m busy.” And we had a snowstorm in Canada, I couldn’t get my Canadian pianist down, so we had to do the gig without him.

But fortunately we had Bucky. The reason he was booked, the guy wanted him of course, to play, Jones, but he’d made a record with Ernestine Anderson and she was on the gig with us. So we had to accompany Ernestine without Hank. He was the greatest pianist. Well he was another Dick Hyman, of that caliber. Oscar Peterson caliber. But he had that reputation, which was so sad.
